title: C
tagline: The language close to the machine
description: C is the language of operating systems, embedded chips and the interpreters of other languages: small, fast, and close to the hardware. Starting from the first program, the course covers types, input and output, decisions, loops, functions and arrays, strings, pointers, memory you allocate and free yourself, structures and linked lists, the bugs C lets you make and how to catch them, bit operations, binary data and files, the preprocessor and programs in several files, function pointers, undefined behaviour, how C turns into assembly, a hash table of your own, and finally the advanced language: variadic functions, struct layout and bit fields, modern C from C11 to C23, error-handling patterns, and threads with atomics, then the practice of real C: dynamic strings, generic containers, dates, command-line tools, safe integer arithmetic and random numbers. Every lesson has checked practice compiled with GCC, and every milestone ends with five projects, from small to large.

milestones.title: First Steps
milestones.blurb: How C builds, variables and types, printf and scanf, operators, and decisions.

lessons.title: C and How It Builds
lessons.summary: C is a small, fast language close to the machine, created in 1972 to write Unix. A C program is text that a compiler turns into machine code in steps - preprocess, compile, assemble, link - and every program starts in a function called main.

lessons.title: Variables and Types
lessons.summary: Every variable in C has a type that decides its size in bytes and what its bits mean - char, short, int, long, long long, float, double, and their unsigned forms. sizeof tells you the size, limits.h the ranges. Always give a variable a value before using it, and use const for values that never change.

lessons.title: printf and scanf
lessons.summary: printf prints with a format string where each % specifier stands for a value - %d, %f, %c, %s, %zu, %x - with optional width and precision. scanf reads input with the same kind of specifiers, into variables whose addresses you pass with &, and returns how many values it managed to read, which you should always check.

lessons.title: Operators and Expressions
lessons.summary: C's arithmetic works on the types you give it - dividing two ints throws away the fraction, % gives the remainder, and mixing int and double converts to double. Casts convert on purpose. Increment, compound assignment and precedence work as in most languages, and signed overflow is a bug the language does not catch.

lessons.title: Making Decisions
lessons.summary: if and else choose what runs, using comparisons that give 1 (true) or 0 (false). Combine conditions with &&, || and !, which stop as soon as the answer is known. bool comes from stdbool.h. switch picks among whole-number cases - remember break - and the ternary operator chooses between two values.

milestones.title: Loops, Functions and Arrays
milestones.blurb: Loops, functions and prototypes, scope and static, arrays, strings as char arrays, and the string library.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: while repeats while a condition holds, for packs the start, the test and the step into one line, and do-while always runs once. break leaves a loop and continue skips to the next round. Watch for off-by-one mistakes and loops that never end.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: A function has a return type, a name and parameters. Arguments are copied into the parameters, so a function cannot change the caller's variables. A prototype declares a function before its definition, and every call gets its own frame on the stack.

lessons.title: Scope, Lifetime and static
lessons.summary: Scope is where a name can be used; lifetime is how long the variable exists. Locals live for one call, globals for the whole run. static on a local keeps it alive between calls, and static on a global or function hides it inside its file. Uninitialised locals hold garbage.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: An array is a row of values of one type, side by side in memory, indexed from 0. C never checks the index, so going past the end is a silent bug. sizeof gives an array's length only where it was declared; a function receives just the address, so pass the length too. Two-dimensional arrays are arrays of rows.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.summary: A C string is an array of chars ending in a zero byte, '\0', which is how every string function knows where the text stops. A literal like "hi" is three bytes. Strings cannot be compared with == or assigned with =. Read a line with fgets, which keeps the new line, and loop over characters until the '\0'.

lessons.title: The String Library
lessons.summary: string.h has strlen, strcmp, strchr, strstr and memcpy. Copying and joining text safely means knowing the buffer size - snprintf is the safe tool, while strcpy and strcat trust you. ctype.h classifies and converts characters, and strtol turns text into numbers and tells you where it stopped.

milestones.title: Pointers
milestones.blurb: Addresses and pointers, pointers and arrays, pointers as parameters, const, and pointers to pointers.

lessons.title: Addresses and Pointers
lessons.summary: Every variable lives at an address in memory. & gives a variable's address, a pointer variable stores one, and * follows it to the value there. A pointer's type says what it points at. NULL means "points at nothing", and following NULL or a pointer that was never set crashes the program or worse.

lessons.title: Pointers and Arrays
lessons.summary: An array's name turns into a pointer to its first element. Adding 1 to a pointer moves it by one element, not one byte, so p[i] is exactly *(p + i). Pointers can walk through arrays and strings, subtracting two pointers gives the distance between them, and a pointer just past the end is allowed as a stopping point.

lessons.title: Pointers as Parameters
lessons.summary: Passing a variable's address lets a function change it, which is how swap works and why scanf needs &. Out-parameters return extra results, with the return value saying whether it worked. Never return the address of a local variable - it dies when the function returns.

lessons.title: const and Pointers
lessons.summary: const marks something as read-only, and with pointers there are two things it can protect. const int *p cannot change what it points at; int *const p cannot point anywhere else. Taking const pointers in functions that only read documents the promise, lets callers pass read-only data, and turns accidental writes into compile errors.

lessons.title: Pointers to Pointers and argv
lessons.summary: A pointer is a variable too, so it has an address, and a pointer to a pointer (char **) lets a function move the caller's pointer. An array of strings is an array of char pointers, and main's argc and argv are exactly that - the words typed after the program's name. Sorting strings means swapping pointers, not text.

milestones.title: Memory and Structures
milestones.blurb: malloc and free, growing arrays, structures, typedef, enum and union, linked lists, and the memory bugs to avoid.

lessons.title: malloc and free
lessons.summary: Stack memory disappears when a function returns and must have a size known in advance. The heap gives memory of any size that lasts until you free it. malloc returns NULL when it fails, calloc clears the memory, and every malloc needs exactly one free - never zero, never two.

lessons.title: Growing Arrays with realloc
lessons.summary: realloc resizes a heap block, moving it if it has to. Assign its result to a temporary so a failure does not lose the old block. A growing array keeps a length and a capacity and doubles the capacity when it is full, so adding stays fast on average - the same trick as Python lists and C++ vectors.

lessons.title: Structures
lessons.summary: A struct groups named fields of different types into one value. Fields are reached with a dot, or with an arrow through a pointer. Structs are copied when assigned or passed, so large ones go by pointer. The compiler adds padding between fields so each one sits at an address that suits it.

lessons.title: typedef, enum and union
lessons.summary: typedef gives a type a new name, often used to drop the word struct. enum names a set of integer constants and makes switch statements readable. A union stores one of several types in the same memory, and a tagged union pairs it with an enum saying which one is there.

lessons.title: Linked Lists
lessons.summary: A linked list is a chain of nodes on the heap, each holding a value and a pointer to the next, ending in NULL. Adding at the front is instant and nothing ever has to move, but finding the nth element means walking the chain. Inserting and removing use a pointer to the link being changed, and freeing the list walks it once.

lessons.title: Memory Bugs
lessons.summary: Overflows, use after free, double frees, leaks and uninitialised reads often run without any visible problem - until they don't. AddressSanitizer adds checks around every memory access and reports the exact line, and Valgrind does it without rebuilding. Warnings and simple habits prevent most of them in the first place.

milestones.title: Bits, Files and the Preprocessor
milestones.blurb: Bitwise operators, fixed-width integers and binary data, files, the preprocessor, and programs in several files.

lessons.title: Bitwise Operators
lessons.summary: & | ^ and ~ work on each bit separately, and << and >> slide bits left and right. With a mask you can test, set, clear and flip single bits, which is how flags, permissions and hardware registers are handled. Shift unsigned values, and keep shift counts below the width of the type.

lessons.title: Fixed-Width Integers and Binary Data
lessons.summary: The size of int and long depends on the system, so stdint.h gives types of exact sizes like uint8_t and int64_t, printed with the macros in inttypes.h. Writing a number's bytes in a fixed order with shifts makes data that every machine reads the same way, whatever its endianness.

lessons.title: Files
lessons.summary: fopen opens a file and returns a FILE pointer, or NULL with errno saying why. The familiar fprintf, fgets and fscanf work on any FILE, and stdin, stdout and stderr are FILEs too. fwrite and fread move raw bytes, fseek and ftell move around in a file, and every opened file must be closed.

lessons.title: The Preprocessor
lessons.summary: Before compiling, the preprocessor runs the lines starting with #. #include pastes in a file, #define replaces names with text, and #if keeps or drops code. Macros are text replacement, not functions, so parenthesise everything and avoid arguments with side effects. assert checks your assumptions while you develop.

lessons.title: Programs in Several Files
lessons.summary: Real programs split into modules - a header (.h) declaring what a module offers and a .c file defining it. Each .c file compiles on its own, and the linker joins them, matching declarations to definitions. extern shares a variable, static keeps things private, and make rebuilds only what changed.

milestones.title: C Close to the Machine
milestones.blurb: Function pointers and qsort, undefined behaviour, how C becomes assembly, the standard library, and a hash table.

lessons.title: Function Pointers and qsort
lessons.summary: A function has an address too, and a function pointer can be stored, passed and called. That lets code take behaviour as a parameter - qsort sorts anything given a comparison function, and tables of function pointers replace long switch statements. A void * parameter lets callbacks carry data of any type.

lessons.title: Undefined Behaviour
lessons.summary: For some mistakes the C standard sets no rules at all - signed overflow, out-of-bounds access, using freed memory, dividing by zero. The optimiser assumes they never happen and builds on that assumption, so their effects can be strange and far away. Learn the list, compile with warnings, and test with sanitizers.

lessons.title: How C Becomes Assembly
lessons.summary: Each C construct turns into a few machine instructions. Locals live in registers or on the stack, arguments arrive in registers, if and loops become compares and jumps, and array indexing becomes an address calculation. Reading compiler output shows what your code costs and what the optimiser does with it.

lessons.title: The Standard Library Tour
lessons.summary: The C standard library is small but covers the basics - input and output, strings, memory, maths, time, random numbers, sorting, characters and errors. Knowing what is there saves rewriting it. Beyond it, POSIX adds the operating system's services, and C23 brings a few modern conveniences.

lessons.title: Building a Hash Table
lessons.summary: A hash table finds a value by its key in about constant time. A hash function turns the key into a number, which picks a bucket in an array; keys that land in the same bucket are chained in a short linked list. When the table gets too full it grows and every entry moves to its new bucket. It is the structure behind Python's dict.

milestones.title: Advanced C
milestones.blurb: Variadic functions, struct layout and bit fields, modern C from C11 to C23, error-handling patterns, and threads with atomics.

lessons.title: Variadic Functions
lessons.summary: Functions that take any number of arguments - how printf does it, va_list, va_start, va_arg and va_end, telling the function how many arguments came (a count, a sentinel or a format), default argument promotions, va_copy, wrapping vsnprintf, and letting the compiler check format strings.

tasks.title: Join strings into a new buffer

lessons.title: Struct Layout, Alignment and Bit Fields
lessons.summary: How a struct sits in memory - alignment and padding, sizeof and offsetof, ordering fields to save space, _Alignof and _Alignas, flexible array members for variable-sized structs, bit fields for packed flags, and why binary files need explicit layouts.

tasks.title: Pack a colour into bit fields

lessons.title: "Modern C: C11, C17 and C23"
lessons.summary: The newer parts of C - designated initializers and compound literals, anonymous structs and unions, _Static_assert, _Generic for type-based dispatch, _Noreturn, and a tour of C23 (bool, true and false as keywords, nullptr, typeof, constexpr, auto, attributes, digit separators and #embed).

lessons.title: Error Handling Patterns
lessons.summary: How C programs report and recover from failure - return codes and out-parameters, errno with strerror and perror, an error enum with messages, cleaning up with a single goto exit, assert for programmer mistakes, and setjmp and longjmp for jumping out of deep calls.

tasks.title: Load a file with one cleanup path

lessons.title: Threads and Atomics
lessons.summary: Running C code in parallel - C11 threads with thrd_create and thrd_join, passing arguments and results, data races, mutexes with mtx_lock, atomic variables from stdatomic.h, condition variables, and how POSIX threads and Windows threads map to the same ideas.

milestones.title: C in Practice
milestones.blurb: Dynamic strings, generic code with void pointers, time and dates, command-line tools, safe integer arithmetic, and random numbers for simulations.

lessons.title: Dynamic Strings
lessons.summary: Building text of any length safely in C - why fixed char arrays run out, a growable string buffer with length and capacity, appending with realloc, a printf-style append with vsnprintf that measures before it writes, handing ownership of the result to the caller, and the common string-building bugs this design prevents.

lessons.title: Generic Code with void Pointers
lessons.summary: Writing one container or algorithm for every type in C - void pointers and element sizes, copying with memcpy, a generic swap, a growable vector that stores any element type, comparison callbacks as qsort and bsearch use them, the type safety you give up, and macros that give some of it back.

lessons.title: Time and Dates
lessons.summary: Working with time in standard C - time_t and time, breaking it into struct tm with gmtime and localtime, formatting with strftime, building and normalising dates with mktime, differences with difftime, measuring how long code takes with clock and timespec_get, and the pitfalls of time zones and thread safety.

tasks.title: Format a moment, find a weekday

lessons.title: Command-Line Programs
lessons.summary: Writing C tools that behave well in a terminal - reading options from argv by hand, flags with values, the conventions of -h, -- and combined short flags, getopt where it exists, standard input, output and error, exit codes with EXIT_SUCCESS and EXIT_FAILURE, reading lines of any length, and working in pipelines.

lessons.title: Safe Integer Arithmetic
lessons.summary: The integer rules that cause real bugs - integer promotion of small types, the usual arithmetic conversions, signed and unsigned comparisons, size_t and loops that never end, overflow as undefined behaviour versus unsigned wrap-around, checking before you add or multiply, the compiler's overflow builtins and C23's ckd_add, and safe size calculations for malloc.

tasks.title: Safe sizes for a growing array

lessons.title: Random Numbers and Simulation
lessons.summary: Making and using random numbers in C - rand and srand and their limits, the modulo bias in rand() % n and how to avoid it, writing a small fast generator such as xorshift or a PCG-style one, seeding for repeatable tests, shuffling fairly with Fisher-Yates, random doubles, and a Monte Carlo simulation.
